title: Gateless Barrier, Case 10: Ch'ing-shui: Solitary and Destitute
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher shares a story from the Mumonkan project about a monk named Xingzhui who asks his teacher for help, but is instead pointed towards recognizing his own state of independence and freedom from attachment. This teaching suggests that "alone" and "poor" may not mean what we typically think they do, but rather refer to a state of possessionlessness and inner richness. The story encourages us to trust in our own practice and recognize the treasure within ourselves, rather than feeling desperate or lacking.

sentences.text: I'm happy to share that Ken Oates has agreed to start uploading all the dharma talks, and Talus trained him the other night, so those will be available, thanks to Ken.
And everything else is available, thanks to everybody else, so thanks for being everybody else.
One of the cool things about the form that we do, the way we move around, is that there are pretty much signals for everything that we respond to.
In the prostrations, for instance, there's a second bell at the end of the last one, so you should have joined me.
I hadn't heard the second bell, so we just keep bowing all night until the dawn.
That's the second bell.
I'm kind of joking a little bit, but it's very serious, too.
One of the texts that we chant says something like, don't make up standards of your own, right?
If the bell hasn't rung to say stop bowing, just keep bowing.
The teachers of old would yell at you for stuff like that.
We don't do that.
A couple more forms things while I'm telling you what to do.
For the [unclear: "Tenkins"], the big candle is an offering of light to the Buddha, so you wouldn't really stick a match in a light offering.
We can just use the little matchbox when you're lighting other stuff.
You'll notice we're doing that.
Also, the mudra is an important part of the zazen form.
It's the right hand on the bottom, left hand on the top.
The knuckles are lined up, thumb tips just barely touching.
And there's an aliveness to it.
It's like you're holding a little ball of energy, so it's not just some place to put your hands, it's this special thing.
It's okay to not always make the mudra.
But I think it would be a shame to sit zazen and never make the mudra, because it's part of the zazen form.
You wouldn't quite exactly be doing zazen.
You've been doing meditation, which is nice, but zazen's a particular way of sitting.
When you're standing, it's the same: the right hand's always on the bottom, or on the outside.
Standing, it's right about the belly button, the solar plexus.
Forearms are more or less parallel.
So it has this nice thing.
Thanks for asking.
Anyway, back to what I'm supposed to be doing.
Tonight we reached double digits in the Mumonkan project.
The 48 stories in the Gateless Gate, or the barrier that has no gate, collection, and we're on case 10.
Here's the story.
*A monk named Xingzhui said to Zhaoshan, Xingzhui is alone and poor.
Please help out.
Zhaoshan said, Reverend Xingzhui, Xingzhui.
Xingzhui said, yes.
And Zhaoshan said, you have already drunk three cups of wine, the finest wine in China.
And yet you still say that you have not moistened your lips.*
So in this story, Xingzhui is the student and Zhaoshan is the teacher, and actually our long-term student and teacher.
Presumably the monk has been in this [unclear: "modest"] story for a long time.
They know each other very well.
Sometimes it's a visiting monk.
So it's helpful to get that part of the story back, the backstory.
A student named Xingzhui said to the teacher, Zhaoshan, Xingzhui, meaning I, is alone and poor.
Please help out.
The teacher, Zhaoshan, said, Reverend Xingzhui, Xingzhui.
The student said, yes.
And the teacher said, you have already drunk three cups of wine, the finest wine in China, and yet you still say that you have only moistened your lips.
Not really much is known about the student, Xingzhui.
But the teacher, Zhaoshan, was an important teacher in the ninth century in China.
I don't really know much about him personally, but it's said in the book that he was important in sort of standardizing the way the koans were presented.
And in fact, he's credited as one of the two founding teachers of Soto Zen, of our school.
And Soto, here's the language layers: Soto is the Japanese voicing of Sao Dung, Sao Dung.
The first character is for this teacher, Sao, so he's the Sao in Sao Dung.
The second character, Dung, is for Dongshan, who I've heard a lot more about.
So anyway, an important teacher and his long-term student, having an exchange.
Here we have a monk proclaiming something and asking for help.
He refers to himself by name, which is interesting, and not uncommon, a way of getting a little out of the sticky trap of me, me, me, me.
You could refer to yourself in the third person.
It should sound funny, but it actually might help you calm down a little bit.
It's such a different thing to say "I'm so upset" versus "Oh, Tim is upset today."
You're like, oh, poor Tim, he'll feel better soon, right?
As opposed to "I'm upset," which is like, okay, universe, you need to give me all the stuff I want and fix me and everything.
So he refers to himself in the third person and says, I'm alone and poor, please help.
The "please help" is interesting.
It's hard to tell in these stories if that's an actual straight-up request for some assistance, some guidance, or a playful jab at the teacher, more along the lines of, I've got it, don't I?
It's more like that.
And it's hard to tell what he means by alone and poor.
What is he saying?
I'm alone and poor.
Is that a problem?
Is that a good thing?
Is that a bad thing?
It doesn't sound so nice to us, although we all value our solo time, I think.
When we feel alone, it's maybe not such a great thing.
And although I think, because of our collective zeitgeist, we may all claim to be not so seduced by the material world, we would all of us very much not like to be poor.
So it sounds like a bad thing: I'm lonely and broke.
Please help out.
There's a gentleman sitting on the steps that come out of our emergency entrance, just outside the garden wall, this afternoon.
I've seen him there two or three times before, and I assume he's experiencing homelessness.
I said, good to see you again.
And he said the same thing he said last time I saw him, which was, is it okay that I'm here?
I said, so fine, the least we can do.
How's your day going?
And he said, could be worse.
And he said, and I'm sorry to be so negative.
I was like, gosh, I don't know what's going on for you, but you can be however you are.
So it seems like alone and poor is probably not a good thing, and he's asking for help.
How can I not be so alone and poor?
Poor is probably not materially poor.
These are monastics.
I may be poor in spirit, or poor in energy, or poor in understanding.

But in one comment I read, the translator Thomas Cleary, not so much a dharma teacher but a great translator, who knows a lot about the Chinese culture of the era in which this was written, says that actually, alone and poor is code for a really good thing.
To be alone is to be independent, to be settled, to be sure of yourself, to be comfortable in your own skin.
So it's a little more like, pay attention to me or don't pay attention to me, I'm fine.
Everything's fine.
And Cleary says that poor means free: free from attachments, free from limited ways, total acceptance, no grasping.
That poor here actually means something like nirvana.
Everything has come to rest.
There's a rich literary tradition in Japan, and probably in China too, around the peacefulness of being alone and possessionless, that actually that's a great kind of freedom.
And this goes back to the original monastics, who the literature of Buddhism says were possessionless monks living by rule.
You would have three robes, one bowl, one pair of sandals, and a little medicine if you needed medicine.
That's all you would own.
Although it seems to be true of our practice, and of all world religions, that the way they say it was and the way it was isn't always quite the same.
I have a Buddhist studies book on my shelf that I've really just skimmed, the title of which is Buddhist Monks and Business Matters.
It's about all the possessions and actual businesses that the monks retained an interest in, a little bit like our dear president.
So there is evidence that the possessionless monks sometimes maintained a few things for later, in case monasticism didn't work out or something.
Or for very altruistic reasons, to take care of their families or maintain the social fabric of their village or their town.
Because in the early Buddhist community, when a whole bunch of men from Buddha's village in the Sakya Kingdom all became monks all at once, it actually was a big problem.
It's like all the eligible men going off to war: all the eligible men went off to sit on their butts and do nothing.
So it was a big problem for the women.
It was part of the origin of the Buddhist women's order that they were basically like, screw it, we're not going to just hang around and do all the work.
They went to the Buddha and said, we want to be ordained too if the men are just going to leave.
And the Buddha agreed, reluctantly, but he agreed.
So anyway, there's a long tradition of the nobility of being a possessionless monastic.
And it makes me think of the famous Japanese monk poet Ryokan.
Do you know Ryokan?
Here are a few poems by Ryokan.
Maybe this monk is referencing something like this.
To be alone and poor is a beautiful thing, Ryokan wrote.
*In my little begging bowl, violets and dandelions mixed together as an offering for the Buddhas of the three worlds.*
*In my little begging bowl, violets and dandelions mixed together as an offering to the Buddhas of the three worlds.*
Of course, violets and dandelions were your ordinary flowers, right?
And the few possessions that one had as a noble person of poverty were real treasures to you, too.
Another Ryokan.
This one has a title, "My Cracked Wooden Bowl."
*This treasure was discovered in a bamboo thicket.
I washed the bowl in a spring and mended it.
After morning meditation I take my gruel in it.
At night it serves me soup or rice, cracked, worn, weather-beaten, misshapen, but of noble stock.*
Nice, huh?
He's not going to take that to Goodwill.
But several times in Ryokan's life his stuff was stolen, even though he didn't have much.
He wrote these great post-theft poems, which were one of his inspirational moments.
So here's one of his post-theft poems, and maybe he lost his cracked wooden bowl too.
He wrote,
*Left behind by the thief, the moon in the window.*
*Left behind by the thief, the moon in the window.*
Another one.
I couldn't find it, but another one says something like,
*If only the thief had stayed, I would have offered him the moon.*
So he had this moon theme.
We're getting close to a full moon now, I understand.
My friend, who's a perfectly confident psychologist, was telling me he thinks everyone's really having a hard time because of the full moon coming up.
Maybe that's true.
I was feeling low energy, and he said, well, I know why.
Why?
It's the moon.
Yeah, you do?
Yeah, it's the moon.
The last one from Ryokan.
This one's about the richness, the wealth of aloneness, the wealth of poverty.
There are quite a few like that.
*What is this life of mine?
Rambling on, I entrust myself to fate.
Sometimes laughter, sometimes tears, neither layman nor monk, as an early spring rain drizzles on and on.
But the plum blossoms have yet to brighten things up.
So all morning I sit by the hearth, no one to talk to.
I search for my copybook, and then brush a few poems.*
It's a great sense of plenty of time.
I guess I'll sit there and do poetry until the plums blossom.
He didn't know it on a calendar, or an iPhone.
So maybe that's what the monk in our story, Xingzhui, is expressing.
Or I think I said it right that time, Xingzhui.
Expressing his contentment in the practice.
Great news, teacher, I'm alone and poor.
What help do I need?
That's what he meant.
But all the other teachers I read suggest it's a little more like our first reading.
The monk is feeling lonely and desperate, and doubting himself.
Doubt is a big thing that comes up in monastic practice.
Pretty much you feel in doubt and you believe that nobody else feels in doubt.
That's pretty much how it is.
So it works either way.
Then the teacher calls out to him, calls him by name.
Tim?
Edie?
Carrie?

And this is a great kind of training, to have somebody who's willing to call to you, to notice you, and call your name with energy, and with an expectation that there's no reason why you can't wake up right now.
It's like, Kate, what are you doing?
And Kate can answer, yes, I'm here.
This is bone on bone.
This is very deep connection.
It's not just "hey you," yeah?
Yes, I'm really here.
Really here.
Yes, I trust the dharma.
I trust my practice.
I trust you, teacher.
Even when I'm feeling alone and poor.
Especially then.
I may be doubtful, but I'm not disillusioned.
I'm down, but not out.
Because actually our practice, with our neuroplastic postmodern bias, we think it's fixing us up.
Did you appreciate my question earlier?
Even though we think it's fixing us up, it's actually all about trusting that we're already alright.
So then the final line of the story is interesting.

After the monk presents either "I'm fine" or "I'm not, please help me," and the exchange of his name, and yes, the teacher says, you have already drunk three cups of the finest wine in China, and still you say you have not moistened your lips.
You say you're alone and poor.
You don't realize there's a jewel sewn into your robe.
You don't realize that the treasure is right beneath your feet, right in front of your eyes.
Which is a common trope in religious literature.
All traditions have stories about people who think that they don't have what they need, and they have to go on a little journey to find what they had all along.
So maybe that's what we're doing.
A great example from Buddhism is the parable of the rich man and his son.
This is chapter four of the [unclear: "Low Sutra"].
A little backstory, and then I'm going to share the story with you, and that will be a way of [unclear: "time, I think, for"].
Interestingly, the story is not told by the Buddha.
The story is told by the students.
Maybe they all said it as one, it doesn't say which student says it.

It describes in there that five or six of the primary early students of the Buddha, Kshapa and Magdalana and Ananda and all those guys, were saying to the Buddha, in the Lotus Sutra in which the Buddha reveals new teachings, they're saying that, gosh, we thought we had something of value, but now we see that we were really like somebody who just didn't get it.
They thought they were desperately poor and didn't realize that the true treasures were right at hand.
And that, oh, Buddha makes us think of this story.
So can we tell you this story?
So they actually tell a story to the Buddha to demonstrate that they get this new level of understanding, this deeper way of being.
Not merely Nirvana, but Anyutara Samyaksambodhi, which is great perfect enlightenment that's in the Heart Sutra that we just chanted.
So the Lotus Sutra is a wonderful sutra full of fantastic stories, but it also has a bit of a dig on the early Buddhas built into it.
So this story actually is kind of that too: the early Buddhas are the desperate poor man in the story, and eventually they wake up, thanks to the Buddha's kindness, to the true teachings.
So anyway, here's what they told the Buddha.
I'll try not to comment, but just read the story.
*Suppose there was a man, still young in years, who abandoned his father and ran away, and lived for a long time in another land, perhaps 10, 20, or 50 years.
As he grew older, he found himself increasingly poor and in want.
He hurried about in every direction, seeking clothing and food, wandering farther and farther afield, until by total chance he returned in the direction of his homeland.
The father, meanwhile, all these years, had been searching for his son without success.
And having taken up residence in a certain city, the father's household was very wealthy, with immeasurable riches and treasures.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and crystal beads filled and overflowed from his storehouses.
He had many grooms, and manservants, and clerks, and attendants, and elephants, and horses, carriages, oxen, and goats, beyond number.*
*The father engaged in profitable ventures at home and in all lands around, and had dealings with many merchants and traveling vendors.
And all this time the impoverished son was wandering from village to village, passing through various lands and towns, until at last he came to the city where his father was residing.
The father had been thinking constantly of his son.
But though he had been parted for him for over 50 years, he, the father, had never told anyone about the matter.
He was originally from a different city, so he never told anybody he had this estranged son.
He merely pondered to himself with his heart filled with regret and longing.

He thought to himself that he was getting old and decrepit, and that he had great wealth and possessions, gold, silver, and rare treasures that filled and overflowed from his storehouses, but he had no son.
So that if one day he should die, the wealth and possessions would be scattered and lost, for there was no one to entrust them to.
This was the reason he constantly thought so earnestly of his son.
And he also had this thought, if I could find my son and entrust my wealth and possessions to him, then I would feel contented and easy in mind and I would have no worries.*
*World Honored One, at that time, the impoverished son drifted from one kind of employment to another until he came by chance to his father's house.

And he, the son, stood by the side of the gate, gazing far off at his father, who was seated on a lion throne, his legs supported by a jeweled footrest, while Brahmins, noblemen, and householders uniformly deferential surrounded him.
Festoons of pearls worth tens or tens of thousands adorned his body, and clerks, grooms, and manservants holding white fly wisps stood in attendance, to left and to right.
A jeweled canopy covered him with flowered banners hanging from it.
Perfumed water had been sprinkled all over the ground.
Heaps of rare flowers were scattered about, and precious objects were ranged here and there, brought out and put away and handed over and received.*
It's just this wealth party, you know?
Great.
*Such were the many types of adornments and emblems of prerogative and marks of distinction.
When the impoverished son saw how great his father's power and authority were, he was filled with fear and awe, and regretted that he'd ever come to such a place.
Secretly, he thought to himself, this must be some king, or one who is equal to a king.
This is not the sort of place where I can hire out my labor and gain a living.
I should better go to a poor village, where if I work hard, I will find a place and earn food and clothing.
If I stay here for long, I may be seized and pressed into service in this fine household.
Having this thought* [unclear: "erased from the spot"].
So it doesn't say it, but in other words, he didn't recognize his own father.
He'd been gone for fifty years.
Didn't recognize his father.
The context is a little different, you know?
*So at that time, the rich old man, seated on his* [unclear: "lying throne"]*, spied his son and recognized him immediately.
His heart was filled with great joy, and at once he thought, now I have someone to entrust my storehouses of wealth and possessions to.
My thoughts have constantly been with this son of mine, but I had no way of seeing him.
Now suddenly he's appeared before me, of himself, which is exactly what I would have wished, for I am old and decrepit.
I still care, so though I'm old and decrepit, I still care for what becomes of my belongings.*
He's trying, you know?
*Therefore, the father dispatched a bystander to go after his son as quickly as possible and bring him back.
So at that time, the messenger raced swiftly after his son and laid hold of him.
The impoverished son, alarmed and fearful, cried out in an angry voice, I've done nothing wrong, why am I being seized?
But the messenger held on tightly and forcibly dragged him back.
At that time, the son thought to himself, I've committed no crime, yet I've been taken prisoner.
Surely I'm going to be put to death.
He was terrified and sank to the ground, fainting with despair.
The father, observing from a distance, spoke to his messenger saying, I have no need of this man.
Don't force him to come here.
Sprinkle cold water on his face so he'll regain his senses,* I guess he really did faint, *and then say nothing more to him.
Why did he do that?
Because the father knew that his son was of humble outlook and ambition, and that his own rich and eminent position would be difficult for his son to accept.
He knew very well that this was his son, but as a form of expedient means he refrained from saying to anyone, including his son, this is my son.*
*The messenger said to the son, I'm releasing you now, you may go where you wish.
The impoverished son was delighted, having gained what he had not had before and picked himself up from the ground and went off to find a poor village in order to look for food and clothing.

At that time, the rich man, hoping to entice his son back again, decided to employ an expedient means and send two men as secret messengers, men who were lean and haggard and had no imposing appearance.
Go seek out that poor man and approach him casually.
Tell him you know of a place where he could earn twice the regular wage if he agrees to the arrangement.
Then bring him back here and put him to work.
If he asks what sort of work he'll be put to, say that he'll be employed to clear away excrement and that you two will be working with him.*
*The two messengers set out at once to find the poor man, and when they had done so, spoke to him as they had been instructed.
At that time, the impoverished son asked for an advance on his wages and went with the men to clear away excrement.
When the father saw his son, he pitied and wondered at him.
Another day, when he was gazing out the window, he saw his son in the distance, his body thin and haggard, filthy with excrement, dirt, sweat, and defilement.
So the father took off his necklaces, his soft, fine garments, and his other adornments and put on clothes that were ragged and soiled.
He smeared dirt on his body, took in his right hand the utensil for removing excrement, and assuming a gruff manner, spoke to the laborers, saying,* [unclear: "Keep it your work"]*.
Don't be lazy.
By employing this expedient means, he was able to approach his son at last.
Later he spoke to his son again, saying, Now then, young man, you must keep on to this work and not leave me any more.
I will increase your wages, and whatever you need, in the way of utensils, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, and the like, you must not worry about.
I have an old servant I can lend you.
When you need him, set your mind at ease.
I will be like a father to you, because I am well along in years, and you are young and sturdy.
When you're at work, you should never be deceitful or lazy or speak angry or resentful words.
You don't need to have any faults of that kind in the way those other workers do.
From now on, you will be like my own son.
And the rich man proceeded to select a name and assign it to the man, as if he were a child.*
*At that time, the impoverished son, though he was delighted at such treatment, still thought of himself as a person of humble station, who was in the employ of another.
Therefore, the rich man kept him clearing away excrement for the next twenty years.
By this time, the son felt like he was understood and trusted.* Really good at clearing away the shit, you know?
*And he felt like he could come and go at ease.
And he continued to live in the same place as before.*
*Well, world-honored one, at that time, the rich man fell ill and knew he would die before long.
So he spoke to the impoverished son, saying, I now have great quantities of gold, silver, and rare treasures that fill and overflow from my storehouses.
You will now take charge of the amounts I have and of what is to be handed out and gathered in.
So you will manage this now.
That is what I have in mind, and I want you to carry out my wishes.
Why?
Because from now on, you and I will not behave as two different persons.
You must keep your wits about you and make sure there are no mistakes or losses from the storehouses.*

*The impoverished son, having received these instructions, took over surveillance of all the goods and gold and silver and rare treasures of the various storehouses, but never thought of or appropriated for himself as much as the cost of a single meal.
He continued to live where he had before, unable to cease thinking of himself as mean and lowly.

After some more time had passed, the father perceived that his son was bit by bit becoming more self-assured and magnanimous in his outlook, and that he was determined to accomplish great things and despised his former low opinion of himself.
Realizing that his own end was approaching, he ordered his son to arrange a meeting with his relatives and the king of the country, the high ministers and the noblemen, and the householders.
They all gathered together.
When they all gathered together, he proceeded to make this announcement.
Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son who was born to me in such-and-such a city.
He abandoned me and ran away, and for over 50 years he wandered and suffered hardship.
His original name was Such-and-Such-and-Such, and my name is Such-and-Such.
In the past, when I was living in my native city, I worried about him and set out to find him.
Sometime after, I suddenly chanced to meet up with him.
This is the truth of my son, and I in truth am his father.
Now everything that belongs to me, my wealth and possessions, now belongs entirely to this son of mine.
Matters of outlay and income that have occurred in the past, this son of mine is familiar with.*
*When the impoverished son heard these words of his father, he was filled with great joy.* He was ready.

*Having gained what he never had before,* what he always had, *he thought to himself, I originally had no mind to covet or seize such things, but now these stores of treasures have come to me of their own accord.* Come to me of their own accord.
*World Honored One, this old man with his great wishes, is none other than the Tathagata.* So it's all a metaphor.
So that's the Buddha.
The father was actually the Buddha.
And we, we, are all like the Buddha's sons.

*The Tathagata constantly tells us that we are his sons, but because of the three sufferings, in the midst of birth and death, we undergo burning anxieties, delusions, and ignorance, and we delight in clinging to lesser doctrines.

Today, the World Honored One has caused us to ponder carefully to cast aside our old doctrines and the filth of, and the previous filth of frivolous debate.* Though in our case, cast aside your old views, you know, who you thought you were, what you thought was true.
Because you didn't realize that actually, you are the heir to great wishes, great riches, right?
So, that's the story, the parable, of the rich man and his son.
So, I don't know if that actually has much to do with our case, but I'll seem to hang together what I thought about it.
So do you ever feel alone and poor?
And it's worth noticing that he does ask for help in whichever reading of the story you think of.
He asks for help.
The teacher responds.
And he shows up for that response.
And the teacher reminds him that you've been rich all along, you know.
You've already tasted the finest wine.
You've already touched the depths of your heart.
And yet, you forgot, you know.
For 50 years, you forgot.
So, the math is a little strange, though.
So, if he was gone for 50 years, and then 20 years of shoveling the excrement, and his father's presumably 20 or 30 years older than he is, and some more time when he was managing the storehouses.
So, these are quite old guys.
By the time Dad made that announcement, you know.
So, one hopes that we'll notice before we're 90 that we're actually okay.
We actually have what we need.
We are alone and poor.
And that's fine.

Because of course, you know, whatever it is we think we're trying to accomplish, whatever it is we think we need to have in us or have in our possession, eventually we'll be chanting for you as we slide your body into the oven.
And you won't need any of that anymore, anyway.
But you will have tasted the finest wine in China.
You'll be okay.
We'll cry, but we'll be happy for you, too.
Okay.
I'll stop.

verbatim.text: I'm happy to share that Ken Oates has agreed to start uploading all the dharma talks, and Talus trained him the other night, so those will be available, thanks to Ken. And everything else is available, thanks to everybody else, so thanks for being everybody else. So one of the cool things about the form that we do, the way we move around, is that there's pretty much signals for everything, right, that we respond to. And so, in the prostrations, for instance, there's a second bell at the end of the last one, so you should have joined me. I hadn't heard the second bell, so we just keep bowing all night until the dawn. That's the second bell. You know, in other words, it's actually kind of, and I'm kind of joking a little bit, but it's kind of very serious, too. There's one of the texts that we chant that says something like, don't make up standards of your own, right?

If the bell hasn't rung to say stop bowing, just keep bowing. The teacher of old would yell at you for stuff like that. We don't do that. Oh, a couple more forms things while I'm telling you what to do. One is that for the Tenkins, the big candle is an offering of light to the Buddha, so you wouldn't really stick a match in a light offering. We can just use the little matchbox to light the, you know, when you're lighting other stuff. You'll notice we're doing that. And also, the mudra, you know, is kind of an important part of the Sazin form.

So it's the left, you know, the right hand on the bottom, left hand on the top. The knuckles are kind of lined up. Thumb tip's just barely touching. And there's kind of an aliveness to it. It's like you're holding a little ball of energy or something, so it's not just like some place to put your hands, but it's like this kind of special thing.
